paragraphs.text: Goldfarb et al. (1998) described desmin-related myopathy as a familial disorder. Its features were skeletal muscle weakness with cardiac conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and restrictive heart failure, together with intracytoplasmic deposits reactive for desmin in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. Park et al. (2000) noted that desmin myopathy may be hereditary or sporadic. van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) described desmin-related myopathy as an autosomally inherited skeletal and cardiac myopathy caused mainly by dominant mutations in the DES gene. Gudkova et al. (2013) noted that desmin cardiomyopathy is a rare cause of congestive heart failure that can present as hypertrophic, restrictive, or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and that adult-onset cases are often associated with conduction disorders and a neuromuscular phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Porte et al. (1980) described 3 brothers with progressive myocardial deficiency. Most of their cardiac muscle cells showed massive storage of PAS-negative proteinaceous material. On electron microscopy this material consisted of sinuous filaments 7 to 10 nm in diameter, similar to intermediate filaments. Filament storage coincided with disintegration of neighboring myofibrils. Z-band changes gave rise to rod-like bodies, and Z-band material associated with sarcoplasmic reticulum tubules formed more complex structures. Filament storage and myofibrillar disintegration always occurred in areas of extensive development and involution of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, with relatively high glycogen accumulation. A few skeletal muscle fibers also showed discrete sarcoplasmic reticulum proliferation, glycogen overload, and filament deposits.

paragraphs.text: Wolburg et al. (1982) reported 2 unrelated 32-year-old patients with a congenital, slowly progressive skeletal myopathy. One patient (case 2) also had congenital paresis of the pupillary dilator muscle and cardiomyopathy. Skeletal muscle function became severely impaired in case 1 but not in case 2. Muscle biopsies from both patients showed abnormal variation in fiber caliber, and in case 1 atrophic fibers were grouped in places. Inclusions with dense granular and fine filamentous components, consistent with cytoplasmic bodies, were present in about one-third of fibers in case 1 and about one-tenth in case 2. The biopsies also showed Z-disk streaming or disintegration and subsarcolemmal pure filamentous bodies.

Autopsy of 2 affected members showed numerous cytoplasmic bodies in skeletal muscle, mainly in type I fibers, and smooth and cardiac muscle were also affected. paragraphs.text: Vajsar et al. (1993) reported 2 sibs who developed cardiomyopathy several years before the onset of slowly progressive muscle weakness. Skeletal muscle biopsy showed subsarcolemmal crescents of dark eosinophilic material in both type I and type II fibers. This material stained for desmin and ubiquitin but for no other cytoskeletal proteins. On electron microscopy the deposits were aggregates of granular and filamentous material arising from Z-bands. Follow-up biopsies 6 years later showed more fibers with desmin- and ubiquitin-positive subsarcolemmal aggregates. The authors concluded that these features characterized a rare familial myopathy with an unusual distribution of desmin intermediate filament proteins in skeletal and probably also cardiac muscle.

paragraphs.text: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994) described a large kindred with autosomal dominant distal myopathy. Onset was in early to middle adulthood with gait disturbance due to distal leg weakness. Over 5 to 10 years the disease spread to all extremities and to the bulbar, respiratory, and facial muscles. Cardiac involvement was frequent, with arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and congestive heart failure, and led to premature death. EMG showed prominent spontaneous activity, short-duration motor unit potentials, and polyphasia. Muscle biopsies from several family members at different stages of the disease showed desmin storage and autophagocytosis. The authors noted that this distal myopathy differed from phenotypically similar disorders in its rapid progression, fatal course, and pathologic features.

paragraphs.text: Melberg et al. (1999) studied a Swedish family with myopathy and cardiomyopathy. They examined 21 family members neurologically and cardiologically and reviewed the charts of 2 deceased affected patients. Twelve patients had myopathy. Weakness was axial in mildly affected patients, axial and predominantly distal in moderately affected patients, and generalized in severely affected patients. paragraphs.text: Piñol-Ripoll et al. (2009) reported a girl who was the only child of consanguineous (uncle-niece) parents. She had recurrent syncope from age 6 months, initially attributed to an accessory conduction pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), and progressive syncopal, presyncopal, and cyanotic attacks from age 3 years. At age 15 she had a long narrow face, bilateral facial weakness, ptosis, and symmetric scapular winging. She had atrophy of the masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid, and trunk muscles, as well as pes cavus, mild shoulder girdle and distal limb weakness, and hypoactive reflexes. Creatine kinase was elevated 2-fold. EMG showed complex repetitive discharges, some myotonic discharges, and a myopathic pattern. Holter monitoring showed monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, QT prolongation, and second-degree AV block, and she required an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator and a pacemaker. At 18 years she had recurrent ventricular tachyarrhythmias, mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 45%), right ventricular dilatation, markedly enlarged atria, and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Skeletal weakness progressed rapidly, and diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss suggested involvement of intestinal smooth muscle. She died of cardiac failure before age 21. Deltoid muscle biopsy showed variation in fiber size, and more than 90% of fibers had peripheral deposits of homogeneous eosinophilic material that was Congo red positive and strongly desmin-immunoreactive. Some rimmed vacuoles were present, and electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous material, consistent with myofibrillar myopathy. The inclusions differed from the amorphous patches seen in most patients with dominant or de novo desmin mutations.

paragraphs.text: In a Swedish family with myofibrillar myopathy and ARVC, Melberg et al. (1999) carried out linkage analysis of candidate regions. They obtained a maximum 2-point lod score of 2.76 at marker D10S1752 on 10q and a multipoint peak lod score of 3.06 between markers D10S605 and D10S215, and suggested that 10q22.3 might harbor the defect. Kuhl et al. (2008) re-examined this family with a high-density SNP panel (Affymetrix Human Mapping 10K Array). They confirmed linkage to 10q22.3, found no other region with significant evidence of linkage, and narrowed the critical interval from 10.6 Mb to 4.27 Mb between D10S1645 and D10S1786. The narrowed region contained 18 candidate genes, 17 of which (RAI17, PPIF, C10ORF56, SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPA1B, SFTPA2B, SFTPD, C10ORF57, PLAC9, ANXA11, MAT1A, DYDC1, DYDC2, C10ORF58, TSPAN14, and SH2D4B) lie in the CMD1C region as well. No disease-causing mutation was found in the coding regions of these genes. Sequence analysis also excluded metavinculin (VCL) and ZASP/cypher (LDB3), which flank the linked region. To search for submicroscopic and intragenic deletions, the authors generated hybrid cell lines that carried only the affected or only the normal chromosome 10 homolog. All sequence-tagged sites and exons were present on both homologs. They speculated that regulatory mutations in 1 of the 18 genes from 10q22.3 might cause a heterogeneous spectrum of myodegenerative disorders. Hedberg et al. (2012) noted that no causative mutation had been found in the 10q22.3 region and that the causative mutation in this family lay instead in the DES gene on chromosome 2q35.

paragraphs.text: In 2 members of a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive LGMD2, Cetin et al. (2013) identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the DES gene (c.1289-2A-G). paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness, severe systolic dysfunction, and progressive respiratory weakness without myofibrillar aggregates, Riley et al. (2019) identified compound heterozygous variants in the DES gene. One was a leu190-to-pro (L190P) missense variant inherited from the father. The other was a deep intronic variant in intron 7 inherited from the mother. The father and brothers, who carried only L190P, were clinically unaffected. Because the maternal allele underwent strong nonsense-mediated decay, the desmin present in muscle, which was reduced by 60 to 75%, likely consisted only of the L190P mutant protein.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters with recessive DES cardio/myopathy, Riley et al. (2019) identified a maternally inherited deep intronic variant in intron 7 of the DES gene, in compound heterozygous state with L190P. RNA sequencing and analysis of muscle cDNA showed that the variant created aberrant splicing, inserting an artificial exon/intronic fragment that shifted the reading frame and created a premature termination codon.
